title: Rapid patchflow and backport guidelines for rollouts and LTS channels
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Purpose: Define an operationally-safe, auditable, and fast rollback & hotfix flow for Redwood Inference across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This doc establishes severity criteria, patch-branch conventions, backport prioritization for LTS channels, automated gating, and upgrade tooling integrations so teams can resolve production-severity regressions with predictable SLAs and minimal customer impact.

Scope: runtime, serving, control plane, and console codepaths that affect inference correctness, availability, or data security. Does NOT cover non-production experimental branches or docs-only fixes.

Summary of approach:
- Classify incidents by severity with defined remediation SLAs.
- Create a small, tested patch on a named patch branch and push through an expedited CI/QA gate.
- Prioritize backports to active LTS channels and stable release branches before canaries.
- Use automated tooling where possible (backport bot, shipctl create-release, release-coordinator checklists) and require human approval for high-risk rollouts.

Key outcomes we want:
1) Mean time to safe rollback/hotfix < 90 minutes for S0/S1.
2) Clear owner model for patch creation, QA validation, and rollout gating.
3) Minimal manual steps for low-risk fixes via automation.
4) A reproducible audit trail (PRs, release notes, rollback window) for every emergency change.
acceptance_criteria: Severity matrix validated and published in runbook
Patch branch naming and backport priority are enforced by backport bot in PR template
CI config includes an expedited hotfix pipeline that runs unit + critical e2e + smoke canary deploy
Automated metric gates (error-rate, p95 latency) prevent unsafe rollouts; manual override requires 2 approvers
Auditable log of trigger, PRs, approvals, and release tags stored in release-ops Confluence and linked from the ticket
steps: 1) Triage & Severity assignment by oncall SRE (S0/S1/S2/S3). See Severity Criteria below.
2) Create patch branch from latest GA or LTS tag: patch/<major>.<minor>.v<patch>-hotfix (e.g., patch/1.18.v3-hotfix).
3) Implement minimal fix + test, open PR against patch branch, add labels: hotfix, backport-needed, customer-facing, release-manager-review.
4) Backport ordering: LTS channels (active) -> stable GA -> dedicated customer branches -> canary. Backport bot will attempt cherry-picks in that order and open PRs.
5) Hotfix pipeline triggers: unit tests -> critical e2e smoke -> binary build/immutable image -> staging canary deploy (10% traffic) with 30m watch window and automated metrics checks.
6) If canary passes, escalate to staged rollout (50%) for another 30-60m, then full rollout. Each step requires release manager ACK; S0/S1 require two approvers (Release Manager + Eng Lead).
7) If metrics regress at any gate, automatic rollback to previous tag is initiated by shipctl, and the issue returns to triage for a larger fix.
8) Postmortem: Within 72 hours, author submits a blameless incident report with linked PRs, rollout logs, and follow-ups (backports, test coverage gaps).
severity_criteria: S0 - Catastrophic: widespread data loss, security breach, system unavailable for >50% customers. SLA: Mitigation/Triage T+15m, patch attempt T+60m.
S1 - Critical: Major feature/regression causing significant customer impact (high error rates, severe latency) for production. SLA: Mitigation/Triage T+30m, patch attempt T+120m.
S2 - Major: Partial degradation or isolated customer incidents, workaround exists. SLA: Triage within 4 hours, patch in next release cycle or expedited if regression grows.
S3 - Minor: Non-urgent, cosmetic, or non-production issues. Handled in normal release cadence.
patch_branch_policy: Branch from the exact released tag (not main) to preserve reproducibility.
Keep patches minimal: single logical change per patch PR unless mitigation requires multi-file coordinated change.
Require changelog entry and link to incident ticket; auto-include release notes via release-ops bot.
backport_rules: Backport priority: 1) active LTS branches 2) latest GA stable 3) customer-specific dedicated branches 4) canary/edge branches.
Automated cherry-pick via backport-bot: bot attempts backports in the above order and opens PRs tagged with backport:pending.
Human review required for any backport touching security-sensitive or migration code paths. Set security_review_required = true for those PRs.
If a backport applies cleanly but CI fails on the target branch, escalate to Release Manager for decision; do not merge until CI green or explicit waiver recorded.
gating_and_observability: Define metric gates for canary: error_rate_threshold (2x baseline or +5% absolute), p95 latency increase > 20%, or dropped QPS > 10%.
Automated Grafana/PagerDuty checks during watch windows; failure triggers auto-rollback job in shipctl.
All hotfix deployments must attach a rollout note and an experiment_id so we can query per-rollout metrics in console.
automation_and_tools: Backport-bot (internal): prepares cherry-picks and PRs, adds reviewer and backport labels.
shipctl: release creation, tagging, rollback orchestration, and gradual traffic shifts between versions.
hotfix-pipeline: an expedited CI pipeline with prioritized agents, runs essential tests and smoke deploys only.
release-coordinator checklist (Confluence): a short sequence of steps for operators; release-manager must sign off in the PR.
roles_and_owners: Release Manager: approves rollouts, coordinates communication, signs off on backports to LTS.
Patch Author: creates patch branch and PR, provides test coverage and release notes.
Oncall SRE: triage incident, runs immediate mitigations, owns rollback if automated rollback fails.
QA Reviewer: validates hotfix pipeline outputs and confirms canary health before wider rollout.
Product/Customer Success (optional): notifies impacted customers where relevant.
risks_and_tradeoffs: Faster hotfix lanes reduce validation depth — mitigated by strict metric gates and brief watch windows.
Automated backports can introduce subtle regressions on legacy branches; we require extra scrutiny for security-sensitive paths.
Enforcing LTS-first backports may delay fixes on canary customers; document exceptions for high-priority enterprise customers.
